headline: RBI Holds Repo Rate Steady at 5.25% in August 2026 Policy
intro: The Reserve Bank of India's rate-setting committee met in early August 2026 and chose not to change interest rates, even though the economy is facing pressure from high oil prices and a weak rupee.
what_happened: The Reserve Bank of India's Monetary Policy Committee (MPC) completed its third bi-monthly meeting of the financial year on August 5, 2026. All six members voted unanimously to leave the repo rate unchanged at 5.25%, keeping a 'neutral' policy stance. The Standing Deposit Facility stayed at 5.00%, and the Marginal Standing Facility and Bank Rate stayed at 5.50%. Governor Sanjay Malhotra said the RBI wanted clearer signs of where inflation was heading before making any change to rates.
key_facts: Repo rate held at 5.25% for a second straight policy meeting.
The RBI raised its FY27 growth forecast slightly, from 6.6% to 6.7%.
The RBI's inflation forecast for FY27 was trimmed slightly to around 5.0%.
The decision came amid tension in West Asia, volatile oil prices, and an uneven monsoon.
The next policy meeting is scheduled for October 5-7, 2026.
why_important: The repo rate is the interest rate at which the RBI lends short-term funds to commercial banks. When the RBI changes this rate, it influences the interest rates banks charge on loans and offer on deposits across the whole economy. Holding the rate steady signals that the RBI is being cautious rather than aggressive, choosing to wait and watch rather than react immediately to global shocks.
economic_impact: Loan EMIs (home loans, car loans, business loans) are unlikely to change in the near term since banks' lending rates are closely tied to the repo rate. The decision also reflects the RBI's preference for using other tools -- such as managing foreign exchange reserves -- to support the rupee, rather than raising interest rates, which could slow down economic growth.
impact_on_people: For students and young professionals, this means borrowing costs (education loans, personal loans) should stay roughly the same for now. For businesses, stable rates mean predictable borrowing costs, which supports continued investment and hiring.
simple_explanation: Think of the repo rate as the 'wholesale' interest rate the RBI charges banks. If it goes up, loans become costlier for everyone; if it goes down, loans become cheaper. By keeping it unchanged, the RBI is essentially saying 'let's wait and see' before making the cost of borrowing more expensive or cheaper.
source: Forbes India, Flattrade Kosh, Business Standard
